summary: ModSafetyModule is an stkAAVE-style backstop: stake a token for 18-decimal shares, earn a MasterChef-style reward stream, signal a cooldown and exit inside a short window, and let the owner slash a capped fraction of the pot to a recovery fund. The two properties the block exists for — rewards that accrue to stakers and capital that cannot leave when a slash is needed — both fail. The share token inherits ERC20Base transfers with no settlement hook, so anyone can stake once and walk the shares through fresh addresses, claiming the whole reward history at every hop until the reward balance (and, when the reward token is the stake token, the principal) is gone (SAFETYMODULE-1); the same transferability lets a staker keep a pre-warmed address in-window and exit instantly, defeating the cooldown (SAFETYMODULE-3). The slash cap is per call with no epoch accounting, timelock or recipient restriction, so the owner — which the catalog wires to the governor, a body the locked stakers cannot vote in — can drain ~100% of the pot to itself in one transaction while stakers are locked (SAFETYMODULE-2, SAFETYMODULE-4). Emissions are unlinked from funding, fund() is permissionless and can halt or retroactively re-open the schedule, and the sink port strands tokens. It is not safe to deploy as-is for third-party funds; it needs a transfer hook that settles rewards and carries cooldown state, a cumulative slash cap, and a funded-reserve check before it is a backstop rather than a honeypot.

findings.title: Share transfers skip reward settlement: stake once, then loop transfer-to-fresh-address + claim() to drain the entire reward pot (and principal if rewardToken == stakeToken)
findings.where: ERC20Base.transfer()/transferFrom()/_move() common.sol L78-L100 (not overridden), _settle() L90-L92, claim() L94-L105, stake() rewardDebt L117
findings.detail: Reward accounting is MasterChef-style: a user's claimable amount is balanceOf*accRewardPerShare/1e18 - rewardDebt, and rewardDebt is only written in claim(), stake() and redeem(). The share token inherits ERC20Base unchanged, so transfer() moves balanceOf without touching rewardDebt or pendingReward. A receiving address that has never staked has rewardDebt == 0, so on its first claim() it is credited balance*accRewardPerShare/1e18 — the full accumulator since deployment, i.e. rewards that were already paid to (or are still owed to) every other staker. Because claim() then sets the receiver's rewardDebt and the shares can be moved again, the same shares can be walked through an unbounded series of fresh addresses, each one claiming the whole history again. claim() caps each payment at rewardToken.balanceOf(this), so the loop drains every funded reward token; if the reward token is also the stake token (the stkAAVE shape the block is named after) it drains stakers' principal too, because that balance is the same pot. The sender side is also broken: after transferring out, (balanceOf*acc)/1e18 - rewardDebt underflows in _settle(), so claim(), stake() and redeem() all revert for that address — an honest user who moves stkMOD to a cold wallet or an LP pool bricks their original address.
findings.exploit: Precondition: the module has run for a while so accRewardPerShare > 0 and reward tokens are funded. 1) Attacker stakes X (rewardDebt = X*acc, so they cannot claim history themselves). 2) transfer(fresh1, X). 3) From fresh1 call claim(): pendingReward = X*acc/1e18 - 0, paid out (capped at the contract's reward balance). 4) transfer(fresh2, X) from fresh1, claim() from fresh2 — same payout again. 5) Repeat until rewardToken.balanceOf(module) == 0. 6) Move the shares to an address with an open unstake window (SAFETYMODULE-3) and redeem X. If rewardToken == stakeToken the loop keeps paying out of totalStaked until the module holds nothing and every other staker's redeem() reverts on PUSH_FAILED.
findings.recommendation: Override _move() in ModSafetyModule to _update(), _settle(from), _settle(to), move the balance, then rewrite rewardDebt for both parties (or make the share token non-transferable). Also fix the sender side by letting _settle() compute against the post-transfer balance only after rewardDebt has been re-based.

findings.title: The slash cap is per call, not per epoch: the owner can call slash() repeatedly in one transaction and drain ~100% of the pot to itself while stakers are locked behind the cooldown
findings.where: slash() L156-L163, setRecoveryFund() L172-L174, constructor cap L51, setTerms() L183
findings.detail: maxSlashBps (<= 50%) bounds a single call against the current totalStaked, but nothing bounds the number of calls, tracks slashed-to-date, or enforces a delay between slashes. With the catalog default of 3000 bps, n successive calls leave 0.7^n of the pot; 20 calls in one transaction leave 0.08%. The recipient is recoveryFund, and when that optional port is not wired (the catalog leaves it optional) it defaults to owner — the slasher pays itself. Even when a recovery fund is wired, the owner can setRecoveryFund(self) in the same transaction. There is no timelock, no pause, no cooldown pause, and stakers who have not already signalled cannot exit for cooldownPeriod (10 days by default), so the 'capped fraction' promised in the docs and catalog summary is not enforced in any meaningful sense. Every staker's principal is fully custodial to the owner key.
findings.exploit: Owner (EOA, or a governor proposal that has passed): 1) setRecoveryFund(attacker) (or leave it unset so funds go to owner). 2) In one transaction call slash(type(uint256).max) 20 times; each call moves 30% of the remaining totalStaked to attacker. 3) totalStaked is now ~0.08% of the original; exchangeRate() collapses accordingly and every staker's redeem() returns dust. Stakers cannot front-run because redeem() requires a cooldown started >= cooldownPeriod earlier.
findings.recommendation: Track a cumulative slashed amount per epoch (e.g. slashedThisEpoch <= maxSlashBps of a snapshot taken at the first slash, epoch length >= cooldownPeriod), or enforce a minimum interval between slashes that is longer than cooldownPeriod + unstakeWindow so stakers can respond. Require recoveryFund != address(0) and != owner, make it changeable only through a timelock, and emit a pending-slash event with a delay before execution. Deploy the governor port behind the timelock block.

findings.title: The cooldown is defeated by transferring shares to a pre-warmed address: cooldown state is per address, transfers do not adjust it, and stake() never resets it
findings.where: cooldown() L121-L125, redeem() L134-L139 and L147, stake() L109-L119 (no cooldownStart write), ERC20Base._move() common.sol L93-L100
findings.detail: redeem() checks only cooldownStart[msg.sender] and balanceOf[msg.sender]. Any address holding >= 1 wei of shares can call cooldown(), and shares are freely transferable, so a staker can keep a rotating set of throwaway addresses each holding 1 wei, with cooldowns staggered so that at every moment one of them is inside its unstake window. To exit instantly they transfer their full position to that address and redeem in the same transaction. With the defaults (10-day cooldown, 2-day window) six addresses staggered 2 days apart give permanent liquidity for 6 wei of stake. Separately, stake() does not reset or weight cooldownStart, so a user already inside their window can stake any amount and redeem it in the same block, earning emissions with zero lock. Aave handles both cases by recomputing the recipient's cooldown as a weighted average on every transfer and stake; this block does neither. Because 'the cooldown is the whole point' (contract header), the block provides no actual insurance guarantee: capital can leave the instant a slash is seen in the mempool.
findings.exploit: 1) Attacker controls addresses A (main) and W1..W6. Each Wi stakes 1 wei and calls cooldown() at day 2*i, then re-calls cooldown() every 12 days, so one Wi is always in its window. 2) A stakes 1_000_000 MOD and farms emissions. 3) A slash tx appears in the mempool (or the attacker simply wants out): A.transfer(Wk, all shares) where Wk is currently in-window; Wk.redeem(all) in the same bundle. 4) The slash lands on the remaining honest stakers only. Variant without helpers: A calls cooldown() with 1 wei, waits 10 days, and during the 2-day window stakes and redeems at will.
findings.recommendation: On every share transfer and stake, recompute the recipient's cooldownStart as the balance-weighted average of sender and recipient cooldowns (Aave's getNextCooldownTimestamp), clearing it when the recipient had none; or make the share token non-transferable. Optionally block redeem() and cooldown() while a slash is pending (see SAFETYMODULE-10).

findings.title: Composition: wiring a token-vote governor as owner lets a liquid minority (or a flash loan) vote to slash the locked stakers to itself, because staked governance tokens cannot vote
findings.where: constructor owner_ L48-L49 (catalog ctor: $input:governor|$owner), slash() L156-L163, setRecoveryFund() L172-L174, setTerms() L181-L187
findings.detail: The intended shape is: MOD is the governance token, stakers lock MOD here for emissions, and the governor block owns the module. But the governance tokens sitting in this contract are held by the module, not by stakers, and stkMOD is a different token, so every MOD staked here is removed from the voting supply. The more successful the safety module is, the smaller the liquid supply that controls it. An attacker who buys or flash-borrows a majority of the remaining liquid MOD can pass a proposal that calls setRecoveryFund(attacker) followed by slash() in a loop (SAFETYMODULE-2), and can precede it with setTerms(365 days, 1 hours, 5000) so nobody can exit during the voting period. Stakers, who are the ones being robbed, have no vote to stop it. If the stake token is instead an unrelated asset the governance-capture risk is the ordinary one, but recoveryFund defaulting to owner means the proposal still pays the governor contract itself.
findings.exploit: State: 60% of MOD staked in the module, 40% liquid, governor quorum measured against liquid voting power. 1) Attacker acquires >50% of the liquid MOD (25% of total) by purchase or flash loan if the governor snapshots at proposal time. 2) Proposes a batch: setTerms(10 years, 1 hours, 5000); setRecoveryFund(attacker); slash(max) x 30. 3) Vote passes on the attacker's own weight; stakers cannot vote and cannot redeem. 4) On execution ~100% of totalStaked is transferred to the attacker.
findings.recommendation: Give stkMOD voting power in the governor (count balanceOf here, or snapshot delegated stake) so stakers control their own backstop; put the timelock block between governor and this module with a delay > cooldownPeriod + unstakeWindow; enforce a per-epoch cumulative slash cap; require recoveryFund to be a fixed, non-owner contract.

findings.title: Using the same token for stake and reward makes claim() pay unfunded emissions out of stakers' principal
findings.where: claim() L100-L103 (available = rewardToken.balanceOf(this)), stake() L114-L115, redeem() L143-L148, constructor L50-L53 (no stakeToken != rewardToken check)
findings.detail: Emissions are never checked against funding: setRewardRate() sets any rate and fund() only tops up a balance. claim() then pays min(pending, rewardToken.balanceOf(this)). When rewardToken == stakeToken — the canonical stkAAVE design, and something a deployer can wire in one drag on the canvas — that balance is totalStaked plus whatever rewards were funded. Any excess of promised over funded rewards is therefore paid from staked principal without reducing totalStaked, so the contract becomes insolvent: exchangeRate() still reports full value, early redeemers are paid in full, and the last redeemers hit PUSH_FAILED. Promised exceeding funded is easy to reach: an owner over-setting the rate, a lapse in topping up, or the fund() gap-accrual bug in SAFETYMODULE-7; with SAFETYMODULE-1 it is total loss.
findings.exploit: 1) Deploy with stakeToken == rewardToken == MOD, setRewardRate(1e18/s), fund(100e18, 30 days) (underfunded). 2) Stakers deposit 1_000_000e18. 3) After the 100 MOD of rewards are gone, claim() keeps succeeding because balanceOf(this) is ~1_000_000e18; each claim moves principal to the claimant. 4) totalStaked is unchanged, so redeem() quotes full value; the final redeemers revert. Anyone who claims early is paid with other stakers' MOD.
findings.recommendation: Track funded rewards in a separate accounting variable (rewardReserve += amount in fund(), -= amount in claim()) and cap claims at rewardReserve rather than balanceOf; alternatively require stakeToken != rewardToken in the constructor and in the catalog wiring.

findings.title: setTerms() has no upper bound on cooldownPeriod and applies retroactively to in-flight cooldowns, so the owner can trap every staker indefinitely or silently close open windows
findings.where: setTerms() L181-L187, redeem() L137-L138, redeemableAt() L127-L132
findings.detail: redeem() recomputes opens/closes from the live cooldownPeriod and unstakeWindow at call time. Raising cooldownPeriod from 10 days to 20 days after users signalled moves their opening date out by 10 days; setting it to 100 years freezes every position permanently, with no timelock and no event. The only floors are unstakeWindow >= 1 hour and maxSlashBps <= 50%. An honest owner tuning parameters will also hurt users: lowering unstakeWindow from 2 days to 1 hour instantly expires windows that were open a moment ago. Combined with slash() this is the 'lock then drain' precondition; on its own it is a permanent freeze of user funds by one key.
findings.exploit: 1) 1000 stakers are mid-cooldown (signalled 9 days ago, opens tomorrow). 2) Owner calls setTerms(type(uint256).max / 2, 1 hours, 5000). 3) Every redeem() reverts with COOLING_DOWN forever; no user can leave, and the owner may slash at leisure.
findings.recommendation: Snapshot the cooldown terms per user at cooldown() time (store cooldownEnd and windowEnd, not just the start), cap cooldownPeriod (e.g. <= 30 days) and floor unstakeWindow at something users can actually hit, emit TermsChanged, and apply changes only to cooldowns started after the change (or via a timelocked owner).

findings.title: fund() is permissionless and rewrites periodFinish without settling: anyone can halt emissions with fund(0, 1), and re-funding after a lapse retroactively pays the dead gap, so promised rewards drift away from funded rewards
findings.where: fund() L167-L170, _effectiveNow() L67-L70, _update() L72-L79, setRewardRate() L176-L179, claim() L100-L101
findings.detail: Three problems in one path. (a) fund() has no access control and sets periodFinish = block.timestamp + duration for any duration > 0, while pull(0) succeeds on standard ERC20s. Anyone can call fund(0, 1) to make _effectiveNow() freeze at now+1, stopping accrual for every staker; they can repeat it each block, and the owner has no dedicated setter to fight back (the owner would have to call fund() too, and lose the race). Conversely anyone can extend periodFinish far into the future. (b) fund() does not call _update() first. If emissions ended at periodFinish P and lastUpdate is stuck at P, a later fund(x, d) at time T moves periodFinish to T+d, and the next _update() credits (T - P) * rewardPerSecond retroactively to whoever holds shares at that moment, even if nobody was staked in the gap (it accrues to the current totalSupply). (c) setRewardRate() and fund() are unlinked: the rate can promise arbitrarily more than the balance, and claim() then silently pays partial amounts first-come-first-served, leaving late claimants with pendingReward that may never be honoured. None of these emit events, so the UI cannot tell an operator what happened.
findings.exploit: Halt: attacker calls fund(0, 1) every block (or once, if the owner is inactive): earned() stops growing for everyone. Retroactive gap: emissions end at P; 60 days later a whale stakes and then calls fund(1, 1 days); the next _update() mints 60 days of rewardPerSecond to the accumulator, most of which the whale claims. Underfunding: owner sets rewardPerSecond = 1e18 but funds 100e18; after 100 seconds the first claimant takes everything and later claimants get 0 despite earned() showing balances.
findings.recommendation: Make fund()/notifyReward owner-only (or restricted to a wired emitter), call _update() at the top, and derive rewardPerSecond = (amount + leftover) / duration the way Synthetix StakingRewards does, so rate, duration and funding are one number; require amount > 0; emit RewardAdded; when the reward token is also the stake token keep a separate reward reserve (SAFETYMODULE-5).

findings.title: Composition: as a `sink` port the module receives plain transfers, but stakeToken sent that way is stranded forever and rewardToken sent that way is only released at the owner-set rate
findings.where: catalog provides ['erc20','sink']; stake() totalStaked L113-L115, exchangeRate() L61-L63, claim() L100-L101; no sweep/skim function anywhere
findings.detail: Fee splitters, CDPs, AMMs and lending blocks in this catalog deliver revenue to a sink with token.push(sink, amount) — a bare transfer. This contract has no receive hook and no sweep: totalStaked and exchangeRate() are internal accounting, so stake tokens that arrive by transfer are invisible to every staker and unrecoverable by the owner; a deployer who routes protocol fees denominated in the stake token 'to the safety module' as a staker reward is burning them. Reward-token transfers are at least claimable, but only through rewardPerSecond, so routed fees sit idle unless the owner keeps re-tuning the rate by hand, and once they land they are part of the pot that SAFETYMODULE-1 drains. The 'sink' capability is advertised but not implemented.
findings.exploit: 1) Canvas: feesplitter payee -> safetymodule (sink), fee token = MOD = stakeToken. 2) Each distribute() pushes MOD to the module. 3) balanceOf(module) grows, totalStaked does not; stakers' exchangeRate() is unchanged; there is no function that can move those tokens out. Revenue is permanently locked.
findings.recommendation: Either drop 'sink' from provides, or implement notifyReward()/skim(): reward-token excess (balanceOf - reserve) rolls into the emission schedule, stake-token excess (balanceOf - totalStaked) is credited to totalStaked as a socialised gain (the inverse of a slash) or swept to recoveryFund.

findings.title: Fee-on-transfer or rebasing stake tokens credit assets never received, making the last redeemers unpayable; non-bool-returning tokens (USDT-style) cannot be staked at all
findings.where: stake() L114-L115 (pull then totalStaked += assets), redeem() L143-L148, SafeTransfer.pull/push common.sol L121-L127
findings.detail: stake() adds the requested `assets` to totalStaked regardless of what transferFrom actually delivered, and mints shares on that number. With a fee-on-transfer token the pot is over-stated from the first deposit; with a negatively rebasing token it drifts over time. Because redeem() pays shares*totalStaked/totalSupply and slash() pays from the same balance, the shortfall lands on whoever is last out (PUSH_FAILED) and is not visible in exchangeRate(). SafeTransfer also require()s a bool return, so USDT-like tokens revert on every call.
findings.exploit: 1) stakeToken charges 1% on transfer. 2) Alice stakes 100 (module receives 99, totalStaked = 100, 100 shares). 3) Bob stakes 100 (receives 99, totalStaked = 200). 4) Alice cooldowns and redeems 100 shares -> 100 tokens paid (module now holds 98). 5) Bob can never redeem in full: his 100 shares quote 100 tokens against a 98 balance.
findings.recommendation: Measure balance before/after pull() and use the delta for both totalStaked and share minting; document that rebasing tokens are unsupported; use a low-level safeTransfer that tolerates missing return values if USDT-style tokens are in scope.

findings.title: Redeem is never paused around a slash, so stakers inside their window front-run the slash and shift the loss onto everyone else
findings.where: slash() L156-L163 (immediate, no pending state), redeem() L134-L150, cooldown() L121-L125
findings.detail: slash() executes in one call with no announcement, pending state or pause of redeem(). Any staker whose unstake window is open when the slash transaction appears in the mempool (and, via SAFETYMODULE-3, anyone at all) can redeem ahead of it at the pre-slash exchange rate; the fixed slash amount is then taken from a smaller totalStaked, so the per-share loss of the remaining stakers is strictly higher than the advertised proportional share. The same holds for stake(): nobody stakes into a pool about to be slashed, so the backstop shrinks exactly when it is needed. Aave v3 addresses this with a two-phase slash and a post-slashing period during which cooldown/redeem rules change.
findings.exploit: 1) totalStaked = 1_000; Alice (window open) holds 50%. 2) Owner broadcasts slash(300). 3) Alice sees it, redeems 500 at rate 1.0 first. 4) slash(300) now takes 300 of the remaining 500: Bob's exchange rate is 0.4 instead of the 0.7 the docs promise.
findings.recommendation: Make slashing two-phase (announce with a snapshot of totalStaked and the amount, execute after a short delay), block redeem()/cooldown() while a slash is pending, and compute the slash against the announced snapshot so exits after the announcement do not change the amount taken from remaining stakers.

findings.title: Shares are hard-coded to 18 decimals regardless of the stake token, parameter changes emit no events, and the accumulator truncates to zero for small rates against large supplies
findings.where: constructor ERC20Base(name_, symbol_, 18) L49, _update() L76, setTerms()/setRewardRate()/setRecoveryFund()/fund() L167-L187 (no events)
findings.detail: Shares mint 1:1 with the first stake, so a 6-decimal stake token (USDC) produces shares that wallets display 1e12 times too small; anything that reads decimals() to price stkMOD (the AMM or lending blocks) will be off by that factor. accRewardPerShare adds (dt*rps*1e18)/totalSupply per update, which floors to 0 whenever dt*rps*1e18 < totalSupply — with 18-decimal shares this only bites at dust-level rates, but with 6-decimal shares and frequent updates rewards can round away entirely. No event is emitted for setTerms, setRewardRate, setRecoveryFund or fund, so the console cannot show operators what changed.
findings.exploit: Deploy with stakeToken = USDC (6 decimals): stake(1_000_000) mints 1_000_000 shares that render as 0.000000000001 stkMOD; a lending block using decimals() to normalise collateral under-values the position by 1e12.
findings.recommendation: Read decimals from stakeToken (with a try/catch fallback) and pass it to ERC20Base; emit events for every owner setter and for fund(); consider a 1e27 accumulator scale.

safe_use: Do not deploy this version with third-party stakers until share transfers are either disabled or hooked to settle rewards and carry cooldown state (SAFETYMODULE-1, SAFETYMODULE-3); as shipped, one staker can drain the reward pot and anyone can exit through a pre-warmed address.
Never use the same token for stakeToken and rewardToken with this code: claim() pays from the whole contract balance, so any over-promised emission is paid out of stakers' principal (SAFETYMODULE-5).

Wire the governor port through the timelock block with a delay longer than cooldownPeriod + unstakeWindow, and always wire a recoveryFund that is not the owner; an EOA owner (or a governor the stakers cannot vote in) can slash the entire pot to itself in one transaction (SAFETYMODULE-2, SAFETYMODULE-4).
Treat maxSlashBps as a per-call number, not a lifetime cap; if you must run this code, agree an off-chain policy (one slash per epoch) and publish it, because the contract does not enforce one.

Call setRewardRate only after fund() has covered rate * duration, top up before periodFinish, and watch for third-party fund() calls: anyone can move periodFinish and stop or re-open emissions (SAFETYMODULE-7).
Do not route protocol revenue to this block's sink port: stake-token transfers are unrecoverable and reward-token transfers are not scheduled (SAFETYMODULE-8).
Do not change cooldownPeriod or unstakeWindow while users are mid-cooldown; changes apply retroactively and can close open windows or freeze exits (SAFETYMODULE-6).

Use only plain 18-decimal ERC20s that return bool (the catalog token block is fine); fee-on-transfer, rebasing and USDT-style tokens are unsupported, and 6-decimal tokens produce mis-scaled shares (SAFETYMODULE-9, SAFETYMODULE-11).
